chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad al-Qummi said: We were informed by Muhammad ibn Ali ibn al-Fadl, from Ali ibn Muhammad al-Kisa'i, from Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Faddal, from Ayub ibn Nuh, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the crescents (of the moon), and he said: 'They are the crescents of the months. So when you see the crescent, fast; and when you see it, break your fast.' I said: 'If the month is twenty-nine days, do I make up that day?' He said: 'No, unless two just witnesses testify. If they testify that they saw the crescent before that, then make up that day.'

key_terms.أَقْضِي: Make up (a missed day or extend a month)
key_terms.الْأَهِلَّةِ: Crescents (plural of hilal, referring to the new moon)
key_terms.الْهِلاَلَ: The crescent (specifically the new moon marking the start of a month)

ai.seo_question: How is the start and end of fasting determined by moon sighting in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the mechanism of *ru'yah* (sighting) in Shia jurisprudence, emphasizing that the month remains 29 days by default unless credible testimony confirms the crescent's appearance on the 29th day. It highlights the scholarly principle that the 'making up' of the day is contingent upon the validity of the witnesses' testimony, distinguishing between mere possibility and established fact. This ruling underscores the reliance on empirical evidence and judicial verification (*hukm al-qadi*) in determining the lunar calendar's structure.
